Code/Data excerpt: The unpaid usage of third-party content that currently sustains the business models used by most AI model developers raise the same policy issues that arose in connection with the launch of file-sharing services such as YouTube about 25 years earlier. Given the passage of time, the reemergence of these policy issues in the AI ecosystem presents an opportunity to develop a balanced policy that benefits all stakeholders—encompassing originators, aggregators and users—in the digital creative ecosystem. Rather than rehearsing that familiar back and forth between content owners and intermediaries in the emergent AI ecosystem, it can be more productive to learn from history and experience. The evolution of digital content markets since the early 2000s shows that a property-free environment cannot sustain markets in the original production of creative assets that involve significant production, editorial, distribution and other costs. As illustrated by the development of curated streaming services in the music industry, once the ability to regulate access is restored in some meaningful form, capital reinvests and supports the production, distribution, and licensing activities that are part of any well-functioning market in creative goods. This historical experience conforms to standard economic logic. Just like property rights in tangible-goods markets, IP rights—or technological approximations of those rights—in intangible-goods markets support the revenue flows that in turn support the production, editorial, and distribution activities that sustain a robust creative ecosystem. Without those revenue flows, content would be commoditized to a significant extent and, at least in certain content segments, production entities would be compelled to rely on philanthropy or corporate or government support to survive or would favor low-cost derivative content that uses existing works, rather than investing in more original content protection that involves higher production expenditures. The precise level of economic harm suffered by content owners would be greatest in cases where AI applications generate outputs that are reasonably substitutable for the original content on which the app or associated model had been trained to respond to user prompts. Conversely, in markets where substitutability between original content and AIenabled derivatives is not close, then there may be greater latitude to relax copyright protections through the fair use doctrine or other mechanisms. This economic principle conforms to the emphasis placed by the fair use doctrine—at least, as stated in the last three decisions by the Supreme Court concerning fair use100—on the necessity of scrutinizing closely whether the copyright owner has suffered significant economic harm from the infringing activity.

Code/Data excerpt: The history of copyright-protected content markets in particular, and IPintensive markets in general, shows that secure IP rights typically do not result in prolonged transactional roadblocks that inhibit growth but rather, induce markets to develop solutions that facilitate transactions among a large population of content owners and users.103 While commentators regularly theorize that IP rights inhibit creative production and development, real-world markets suggest otherwise. Specifically, entities with significant stakes at play in IP-intensive markets anticipate the transaction costs that may arise from the widespread deployment of robust IP rights and take action to mitigate those costs and accrue the resulting economic gains. Organizations such as ASCAP, BMI and other collective licensing organizations have long maintained complex systems for administering “public performance rights” to musical compositions in terrestrial radio (among other uses) and now digital radio.104 In the case of digital images, entities such as Adobe, Shutterfly, and Getty already offer micro-licensing options for individual or corporate users.105 In the case of digital video, YouTube offers the largest content owners the option to participate in the ContentID system, which tracks user uploads of proprietary music and then pays a small portion of the associated ad revenues to the copyright owner.106 All of these solutions address to varying degrees the attribution, tracking, and remuneration obstacles that are treated by assumption as almost-insuperable obstacles to deploying robust copyright in creative markets. Given this historical record of transactional innovation, there seems little reason to fear that robust enforcement of copyright in the AI market would somehow depart from historical precedent and stifle development. To the contrary, setting a clear baseline of IP protection as a legal matter would likely induce the development and adoption of transactional solutions that can both remunerate content owners and provide model and app developers with a sufficient pool of content inputs for training purposes. In short: the theoretical sledgehammer of infringement liability will “bring parties to the table” to craft licensing and other payment solutions that bridge the divide between stakeholders who deliver content to the AI ecosystem and stakeholders who aggregate that content for purposes of delivering new technological applications for users.

Code/Data excerpt: In this scenario, while policymakers are primarily focused on whether and how to replicate the Australian model, this paper takes a different approach by questioning the very rationale behind initiatives that compel value transfers from online platforms to legacy publishers. As discussed, such interventions rest on the assumption of a free-riding problem. Namely, that links and excerpts harm news publishers by allowing online infomediaries to divert audience attention, thereby reducing traffic and advertising revenue for the linked sites. This belief is further reinforced by another assumption, namely that, due to the size imbalance between firms and the gatekeeping power of certain platforms, press publishers are inevitably undercompensated. However, according to the empirical studies currently available, the free-riding argument remains largely hypothetical, without consistent support from the evidence. Indeed, the relationship between digital platforms and news publishers involves a two-way exchange of value. Given the positive correlation between website traffic and advertising revenue, publishers may benefit from the very mechanisms often criticized. While platforms become more attractive to users by excerpting content and linking to news sites, legacy publishers, in turn, gain visibility through inbound links that can boost traffic and expand their audience. In other words, any loss in direct visits may be more than offset by an increase in referral traffic. Therefore, while there is a concern that digital infomediaries might harm legacy publishers by diverting online traffic (the substitution effect), there is also a strong argument that, by reducing search costs, they expand the overall number of visits by enabling consumers to discover news content they might not have found otherwise (the market expansion effect).

Code/Data excerpt: In summary, the impact of digital platforms on the revenues of news publishers cannot be predetermined but requires empirical analysis. Rather than labeling victims and perpetrators based on assumptions, policymakers must carefully weigh the welfare trade-off – balancing the benefits of lower search costs for consumers against the potential weakening of incentives for news producers – and assess on a case-by-case basis whether referral traffic compensates for any loss in direct visits. As a result, rather than debating how much press publishers should receive from online platforms or which mechanism would best secure such a revenue transfer, the more fundamental question is whether press publishers should be remunerated at all. Indeed, since the value of referral traffic cannot be overlooked, in some instances it may even be online platforms that warrant compensation for the benefits they provide to news publishers. Additional concerns about compulsory arbitration processes relate to their potential impact on competition in the publishing industry. Because transaction costs discourage bargaining with every publisher, forcing large online platforms to strike deals may lead them to selectively engage only with major publishers that have large audiences. As a result, these mechanisms could increase market concentration and reduce media plurality. By revisiting the economic literature and analyzing the Australian model, as well as its influence on other jurisdictions, this paper argues that the free-riding problem is largely a rhetorical construct, strategically employed to justify a mandated revenue transfer that policymakers are inclined to impose, regardless of whether press publishers have incurred any demonstrable economic harm from the rise of platform-based business models. From the perspective of policymakers, mandating revenue sharing by large online companies appears indeed to be the most convenient means of sustaining subsidies for the publishing industry.

Code/Data excerpt: Despite the close regulatory scrutiny on the issue, empirical evidence on the impact of digital platforms remains scarce. As a result, even in the best-case scenario, legislative initiatives aimed at addressing the allegedly unfair revenue distribution stemming from an imbalance in bargaining power between the parties have been pursued without clear data to substantiate the reported market failure. In fact, the few available studies point in a different direction, suggesting a relationship of complementarity – rather than rivalry – between platform links and news consumption at traditional outlets. Notably, two studies, one by Athey, Mobius, and Pal11 and the other by Calzada and Gil,12 use the 2014 shutdown of Google News in Spain as a natural experiment and reach similar conclusions: they find no evidence of a substitution effect, but rather demonstrate a market-expansion effect. Specifically, the studies show that the shutdown led to a decline in overall news consumption and disproportionately harmed smaller publishers, confirming that newspapers benefit from news aggregation platforms through increased website traffic, as these platforms help consumers discover more content. ... Using a different natural experiment (i.e., a legal dispute between the Associated Press and Google News that resulted in the removal of AP content for seven weeks), Chiou and Tucker similarly find evidence of complementarity between online aggregators and news outlets.15 Moreover, the findings of the study conducted by George and Hogendorn also support the argument that online intermediaries reduce search costs and enhance both interest in and discoverability of news content.16 Their analysis shows that, after Google added a permanent strip of geo-targeted local news links to the Google News front page, the design change increased both the level and the share of visits to outlets local to users’ households, indicating that consumers did not substitute away from direct visits to news outlets.

Code/Data excerpt: In December 2024, the Australian government announced its intention to introduce a ‘News Bargaining Incentive’ aimed at ensuring that large digital platforms contribute to the sustainability of news and journalism in Australia.69 ... The most notable feature of this so-called incentive is that it will apply to large digital platforms that operate significant social media or search services, regardless of whether they carry news content. According to the government, this approach addresses a key limitation of the current Bargaining Code, which allows platforms to avoid their obligations by removing news.70 Citing Meta’s decision to withdraw news content in order to sidestep designation under the Code, the government argued that the effectiveness of the framework is undermined by the ability of digital platforms to circumvent it in this way. In other words, the government has openly expressed its frustration at failing to secure a transfer of economic resources from large platforms to press publishers, despite the introduction of a mandatory bargaining code backed by binding final-offer arbitration. It now appears eager to remedy this by compelling payment, even in cases where no use of news content is made at all. For these reasons, the Australian government’s reform proposal offers the clearest evidence that, in the debate over the impact of digital platforms on the publishing industry, the free-riding narrative is merely a rhetorical device, strategically deployed to justify a mandated transfer of revenue that policymakers appear willing to impose, irrespective of whether press publishers have suffered any demonstrable economic harm from the emergence of platform-based business models.

Code/Data excerpt: However, rather than taking on the challenge of gathering empirical evidence to assess the actual impact of digital platforms on press publishers’ revenues, policymakers have chosen a more convenient path. They have placed the blame squarely on large online platforms, overlooking both the outcomes of national experiences following the shutdown of news services by these platforms and the findings of numerous empirical studies. Within this context, the free-riding narrative functions as a policy bias, instrumental in justifying value transfers from big tech companies to legacy publishers. Furthermore, the argument reveals several theoretical shortcomings. While it rightly acknowledges the crucial role of referral traffic for press publishers, it also claims that publishers are heavily dependent on large platforms to attract audience attention, whereas the platforms themselves are not reliant on news content in the same way. Publishers are thus portrayed as actors caught in a paradox, unable to thrive either with or without digital platforms. This logic is exemplified by the recent Australian reform proposal, which advocates imposing a charge on large platforms regardless of whether they carry news content. Yet such reasoning stands in clear contradiction to the free-riding narrative. If news content is not essential to platforms’ business models, but instead is essential to publishers’ business, then the claim that online infomediaries are unfairly exploiting publishers’ investments becomes inherently inconsistent.

Code/Data excerpt: [From media in Romania]: Regarding economic sustainability, most respondents believe that AI will have little impact on solid editorial teams in the short term. However, in the long run, the improvement of AI tools could replace, for example, live performers or presenters. Everyone agreed that field reporters cannot be replaced at this time and that human journalists are needed to verify information from the scene of events. Additionally, AI is a risk in light of new competitors who might use the technology to cut costs and produce lower-quality content that is still very appealing to the audience. This could lead to decreased revenues for traditional organizations that invest in quality journalism. At the same time, the high costs of traditional media production are recognized as a challenge for long-term sustainability, requiring continuous adaptation to new economic and technological conditions. Some media organizations have tried new ways to generate revenue to ensure economic sustainability, but these have yet to have the expected effect. Most have focused their attention on social media to attract readers to their websites, basing their income on digital advertising. Another issue raised by one of the interviewees was related to the approach to the topics. He runs a highly reputable news site and explained that the classic model through which everyone provides content delivered by institutions is becoming increasingly challenging to operate. A news report received from the police will have approximately the same content on other sites if the journalist does not go on the ground and approach the subject in their way. This could be the solution for people who consume information to turn towards a different kind of content (Table 3). In terms of the economic dimension, most respondents (R1–R4) believe that artificial intelligence does not have a major economic impact on established newsrooms, at least in the short term. However, there are concerns about competitive pressure from new media players that make intensive use of AI and reduce costs through automation. R5 has a more pessimistic view, anticipating a gradual replacement of human functions, while R4 highlights market adaptability and the role of demand as the main decision-making factor. These perspectives reflect differences in the perception of risks, but also in the economic adaptation strategies adopted by newsrooms.

Code/Data excerpt: Governments, businesses and civil society representatives, among others, call for “alternatives” to compete with and possibly replace big tech platforms. These alternatives are usually characterized by different governance approaches like being not-for-profit, open, free, decentralized and/ or community-based. We find that strengthening alternative governance models needs to account for the dynamic effects of operating in a digital ecosystem shaped by ad-driven platforms. Specifically, we explore in this article: 1) how interoperability between the microblogging platforms Threads (by Meta) and Mastodon (a not-for-profit service running on a federated open-source protocol) may foster competition, but also create a risk of converging governance in terms of e.g. content moderation and privacy practices; 2) how openness of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia allows Google Search to appropriate most of the value created by their vertical interaction and how the Wikimedia Foundation seeks to reduce that imbalance; 3) which types of interventions might be suitable to support alternatives without forcing them to emulate big tech governance, including asymmetric interoperability, digital taxes and regulatory restraints on commercial platforms.

Code/Data excerpt: We see that interoperability cannot bridge different governance models. On the contrary, it can come with significant drawbacks to smaller, decentralized players like Mastodon in terms of community-led content moderation and privacy. This may lead to two outcomes. Smaller and community-led alternatives may choose to defederate. If they choose to pursue interoperability with actors like Threads, they are likely to see themselves under pressure to adapt their content moderation practices and may undermine their users’ privacy expectations or even adapt their privacy policies.  Hence, instead of contesting the dominant governance model, interoperability might contribute to convergence of the alternative and the incumbent. This seems to echo Mark Zuckerberg’s motivations for federating Threads: Extracting “all of the different content from wherever anyone is creating it” to the benefit of Meta’s ad-driven business model.26 To avoid such an outcome, it is critical that the differences in (bargaining) power to shape interactions are counteracted where possible. This could mean to approach interoperability with asymmetry in mind: For example, interoperability should always benefit the smaller player(s), e.g. remaining optional for them, and it should not undermine their privacy and safety. In the context of mandating social network interoperability, the terms of interoperability need to be negotiated with the requirements of the community-led governance model in mind. This includes addressing the extremely different amounts of resources. Regulation plays a crucial role: The process of negotiating the terms of interoperability may not be left up to chance or the good-will of companies, but must be mandated. At the same time, there may be good reasons for “alternatives” to reject interoperability to preserve their distinct governance models.  This has already become apparent in the context of the interoperability provisions under the Digital Markets Act (“DMA”), the EU’s legal framework to increase the competitiveness of digital markets and address gatekeepers’ dominance. Article 7 of the DMA introduces a mandate for gatekeepers that offer number-independent interpersonal communication services, such as WhatsApp, to provide interoperability of their basic functionalities if requested by any other provider. However, non-commercial competitors like Signal and Threema have made it clear that they are not interested in achieving interoperability with WhatsApp, citing security and privacy concerns.27 There has been a push to expand the DMA’s interoperability requirements to social networking services. This makes it even more urgent to consider the necessary requirements to ensure that interoperability benefits, not undermines, alternatives to gatekeepers.

Code/Data excerpt: Wikipedia content is very valuable for people searching information online. Studies have shown that Wikipedia links appear in 67-86 percent of Google Search results in response to common or trending search queries in both desktop and mobile environments.32 Besides, users of Google Search are much more likely to click on search results if Wikipedia links are among them.33 However, the same study estimates that over 80 percent of Wikipedia visits come through Google, with only a small share coming through direct visits. Through the presentation of the search results, Google can influence the probability of users clicking through to Wikipedia: With so-called Knowledge Panels, infoboxes displayed at a privileged position of the Google Search results, users often get a sufficient answer to their query without accessing additional sources. Knowledge panels display information from Google Knowledge Graph, a knowledge base including a number of sources, including Wikipedia. Removing Knowledge Panels was found to increase the share of users clicking on a Wikipedia link from 11 percent to 21 percent.34 Wikipedia as a project is reliant on financial support and, even more importantly, active communities that ensure that information remains high-quality and up-to-date. Google provided financial support to Wikipedia in the past, with USD2m in 201035 and USD3.1m in 2019,36 expressing its interest in the provision of high-quality content. However, the currently widespread use of large language models (“LLMs”) for information retrieval could reduce Wikipedia’s visibility and also run contrary to its efforts to represent knowledge in an equitable manner.37 Evidence suggests that lower visibility does not immediately trigger a less active community or less high-quality content,38 but it seems plausible that some level of recognition of Wikipedia’s role and relevance to search results and information retrieved is important to maintain an active editorship and willingness to donate.

Code/Data excerpt: To reach a more equal position with technology companies was one of the objectives of launching WME in 2022, a project offering a better (more reliable, faster) access for largescale Wikipedia content users. Open Future, an organization from the open movement, described “understanding and finding this stronger position, a position of equality, [as] the ultimate goal of the Enterprise API.”40 Within the range of objectives also falls to broaden the sources of income for activities such as software development for Wikipedia and related projects and to lower the burden for medium-sized players to get high-quality access to Wikipedia contents.  The specific terms between WME and its “partners” are not public; the website suggests that commercial arrangements start from USD100,000.41 Google was announced as the first paying “partner” (the Internet Archive as a noncommercial project was granted free access at the same time). WME frames this price in terms of fairness and reciprocity: “It will also ensure that donations from our readers will not be used to cover the expenses of large corporate reusers. They will be paying their own way, and also contributing back to the cultural and intellectual commons of humanity.”42 This framing sets WME apart from related strategies usually referred to as freemium in which a free product is free of charge as a strategic choice within a broader for-profit business model. The Wikimedia Foundation has taken steps to limit the impact of WME as a commercial side-project on its community-led governance model. It adopted various principles:43 For example, the revenue of WME as a share of Wikimedia income must not exceed 30 percent, exclusivity clauses or editorial influence are ruled out, WME is infrastructurally separate from Wikimedia projects and all WME outputs need to be licensed as free and opensource software. Another principle states that the existence of paid use should not limit free use which, however, is difficult to observe over time: As WME develops new software, it is difficult to judge how much of that would have been developed also without WME through other ways of financing and to what extent the enter prise-grade software has spillover benefits for the free use of Wikipedia contents.44 WME has not yet contributed through financial profit but it has incurred a cumulative loss of USD1.2m in the last two financial years with revenues of USD 6.6m.45 However, in light of the orders of magnitude of Google profits and also of Wikipedia’s likely contribution, these numbers appear very small. Its contribution might be through the additional software generating spillover benefits for the free version.

Strengthening alternatives requires more than interoperability or money even though they help in many settings Instead, alternatives require a suitable environment to avoid emulating Big Tech by, for example, seeking growth and engagement or imposing a top-down form of governance. Preserving differentiation requires a sound strategy for how to foster these alternatives. This, in turn, requires a clearer understanding of which features of alternatives are particularly important. Such a concept is necessary to determine which restrictions or rules for larger platforms are needed for established alternatives to stay and for new ones to flourish.  A broader concept can build on the interactions that can already be observed. For example, designing interoperability to be asymmetric and to account for the needs of differentiated actors is one possible piece of the puzzle. A combination of stringent digital taxes on commercial platforms48 and financial support for open resources49 another. More interventionist options include to prevent dominant players from entering areas that alternatives with different governance approaches are active in or to restrict certain governance characteristics in certain areas, such as China’s obligation on educational technology companies to become not-forprofit organizations.5

We need to protect artists from AI predation, not just create a new way for artists to be mad about their impoverishment.

Incredibly enough, there is a really simple way to do that. After more than 20 years of being consistently wrong and terrible for artists’ rights, the US Copyright Office has finally done something gloriously, wonderfully right. All through this AI bubble, the Copyright Office has maintained – correctly – that AI-generated works cannot be copyrighted, because copyright is exclusively for humans. That is why the “monkey selfie” is in the public domain. Copyright is only awarded to works of human creative expression that are fixed in a tangible medium.

And not only has the Copyright Office taken this position, they have defended it vigorously in court, repeatedly winning judgments to uphold this principle.

The fact that every AI-created work is in the public domain means that if Getty or Disney or Universal or Hearst newspapers use AI to generate works – then anyone else can take those works, copy them, sell them or give them away for nothing. And the only thing those companies hate more than paying creative workers, is having other people take their stuff without permission.

The US Copyright Office’s position means that the only way these companies can get a copyright is to pay humans to do creative work. This is a recipe for centaurhood. If you are a visual artist or writer who uses prompts to come up with ideas or variations, that’s no problem, because the ultimate work comes from you. And if you are a video editor who uses deepfakes to change the eyelines of 200 extras in a crowd scene, then sure, those eyeballs are in the public domain, but the movie stays copyrighted.

But creative workers do not have to rely on the US government to rescue us from AI predators. We can do it ourselves, the way the writers did in their historic writers’ strike. The writers brought the studios to their knees. They did it because they are organized and solidaristic, but also are allowed to do something that virtually no other workers are allowed to do: they can engage in “sectoral bargaining”, whereby all the workers in a sector can negotiate a contract with every employer in the sector.

That has been illegal for most workers since the late 1940s, when the Taft-Hartley Act outlawed it. If we are gonna campaign to get a new law passed in hopes of making more money and having more control over our labor, we should campaign to restore sectoral bargaining, not to expand copyright.

Code/Data excerpt: Findings show that philanthropic funding is only conditionally conducive to sustainability under capture. Grants enabled survival, professionalization, and audience gains, but rarely produced durable revenue diversity in markets distorted by politicized state advertising, advertiser risk-aversion, and low willingness to pay for news. The program’s clearest contributions were transitional: financing operational and managerial upgrades, supporting product and audience experiments, and providing temporary insulation from hostile conditions. These gains materialized primarily where absorptive capacity and leadership were already strong. Donor-backed networking delivered only partial results, and abrupt donor exit exposed the fragility of post-grant trajectories. The overarching lesson is that donor intervention must be understood as a long-term investment in a difficult-to-visualize public good, namely democratic resistance and opposition, that yields indirect civic returns and, over time, creates the preconditions for tangible market and policy change. Anything less will fail to achieve meaningful or lasting impact.

Code/Data excerpt: Civic institutions—the rule of law, universities, and a free press—are the backbone of democratic life. They are the mechanisms through which complex societies encourage cooperation and stability, while also adapting to changing circumstances. The real superpower of institutions is their ability to evolve and adapt within a hierarchy of authority and a framework for roles and rules, while maintaining legitimacy for the knowledge produced and the actions taken. Purpose-driven institutions built around transparency, cooperation, and accountability empower individuals to take intellectual risks and challenge the status quo. This happens through the machinations of interpersonal relationships within those institutions, which broaden perspectives and strengthen shared commitment to civic goals.  Unfortunately, the affordances of AI systems extinguish these institutional features at every turn. In this essay, we make one simple point: AI systems are built to function in ways that degrade and are likely to destroy our crucial civic institutions. The affordances of AI systems erode expertise, shortcircuit decision-making, and isolate people from each other. They are anathema to the kind of evolution, transparency, cooperation, and accountability that give vital institutions their purpose and sustainability. In short, current AI systems are a death sentence for civic institutions, and we should treat them as such.

Code/Data excerpt: In the case French Competition Authority v Alphabet/Google (in March 2024 the French Competition Authority fined Google 250 million EUR on the basis of French law),27 one of the plaintiff ’s claims was related to the effectiveness of the right or possibility for creators to opt-out of having their content used in LLM training data:  With regard to “Bard”, the artificial intelligence service launched by Google in July 2023, the Autorité found in particular that Bard had used content from press agencies and publishers to train its foundation model, without notifying either them or the Autorité. Google subsequently linked the use by its artificial intelligence service of the content concerned to the display of protected content, by failing to propose a technical solution for press agencies and publishers to opt out of the use of their content by Bard without affecting the display of content protected by related rights on other Google services, thus obstructing the ability of press agencies and publishers to negotiate remuneration.28  This decision by the French Competition Authority represents an interesting articulation of the relationship between the pre-existing copyright legal framework and the development of GPAI models. Code/Data excerpt: Assigning monetary value to news is complicated and the market has clearly failed to set a sustainable price due to information asymmetries and dominant platforms abusing their market power.52 However, using some well-defined and widely accepted underlying principles, there are ways to calculate the dollar amounts that should be paid to news publishers. Publishers themselves sometimes use the CPM (or the cost of advertising to 1,0000 viewers) rates as a basis of comparison or how much they stand to lose by being disintermediated by large language models. This approach can be criticized as valuing the input into the model by the costs imposed on legacy media, rather than how important the news are to the model.  Haaris Mateen has attempted to estimate the value of news to the AI companies by looking at share price movements of tech companies with stakes in generative AI as an indication of how the market values large language models.53 But even if this estimate gives a broad sweep of these companies’ potential revenues and profit, it doesn’t provide a formula to establish the value of news articles or other words used as inputs.  Another approach is to calculate the revenues from online advertising received by a platform, e.g. Google, in a particular country, and attribute a share of it to the contribution of the media content to the overall attractiveness and audience of Google.54 For example, during the negotiations around the Online News Act (C-18 bill) in Canada in 2023, some looked at the revenue Google generated in Canada and settled on 4% of that being given to publishers.5556 A similar study was done by academic Jean-Hugues Roy who analyzed more than two years of Facebook data57 During the time period analyzed, 8.9% of content posted was from news pages, suggesting that Meta owed a substantial sum to Canadian publishers. Relatedly, methodologies to determine the value of the news have been developed by Holder, Maateen, and Schiffrin 58 based on the influential study by Fehr AG for Swiss publishers.59  From a regulatory perspective, two Italian cases are worth mentioning. According to Italian law,60 if the parties involved in a given licensing contract do not reach an agreement on the remuneration of copyrighted content, they can contact the Italian Authority for Communications (AGCOM), the national media and communications authority, to serve as an intermediary. In July 2024, AGCOM set the amount of fair compensation due from Microsoft to the publisher GEDI for the use of its journalistic publications in the Bing search engine.61 In July 2025, AGCOM issued a similar decision, on the amount due by Meta platforms to GEDI, for the year 2022. In both cases, the basis for the calculation is the platforms’ advertising revenues derived from the online use of the publisher’s journalistic publications, net of the publisher’s revenues attributable to the redirection traffic generated on its website by the journalistic publications used online by the provider.62  In the context of AI, it’s important to note that there are different pricing structures for Retrieval Augmented Generation—which adds an external knowledge base to access up-to-date informationcompared to model training and fine-tuning—which relies on a specific dataset to complete particular tasks and maintain output quality.

Code/Data excerpt: According to the MPM2025 findings, in eight EU countries64, there are no ongoing payment negotiations between publishers and platforms regarding the use of media content. In the countries where there are negotiations and agreements have been reached, these are limited. As mentioned above, in France, the competition authority stepped in the process and  regulatory actions intensified in 2024, notably with a €250M fine against Google for violating commitments under the 2019 law on related rights, prompting ongoing investigations into digital platforms French media launched legal offensives against X, Microsoft, and LinkedIn for unpaid content usage, while journalists’ unions secured revenuesharing agreements with Google and Meta.65  As the MPM final report points out, ‘some criticism emerged regarding the exclusion of the most precarious journalists from these benefits in some cases, as well as regarding the opacity of the details of the content and the amount of such agreements’.66 In other countries, such as Denmark, publishers are offering to bargain collectively, hoping to strengthen their position in a relatively small market.67  In Germany, the ground-breaking deal between Axel Springer and OpenAI does not seem to have opened a path for the smaller media outlets:  While German market leaders signed deals with AI Companies, small and independent media outlets risk being increasingly disadvantaged when people shift from using Google Search to relying on AI models since visibility will likely favor larger media companies with licensing deals. This could lead to greater market concentration, as only a few publishers gain prominence in AI-generated outputs.68  The risk that the AI deals only benefit the larger media outlets is also highlighted in France. After the deal signed by Le Monde with OpenAI,  APIG (Alliance de la presse d’information générale) and SEPM (Syndicat des éditeurs de la presse magazine), two press unions representing about 800 titles, asked 25 of the main AI actors (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Bytedance, etc.) to open negotiations on the use of their contents. Surprisingly and quite abruptly, OpenAI refused to negotiate and announced to respect the opt-out decided by these media.69  In Spain, the content of the deal signed between PRISA and OpenAI in 2024 ‘is unknown, [including] the amount that the media will receive for their content, which contributes to the opacity of the digital media sector’.70  The report’s findings, albeit limited in time and scope, highlight several themes. First, market and population size matter: in smaller countries and for less widely spoken languages, AI companies are very unlikely to pay for media content. Second, there is a risk of the exclusion of small and diverse media outlets. Although collective organisational processes are emerging, they have not yet produced substantial outcomes. Third, there is a lack of transparency regarding the terms and conditions of the deals, which is not necessarily justified by the need to protect industrial or commercial secrets. This is particularly concerning given the public interest in transparency in the information sphere.

But it has one disadvantage: because the bargaining power is normally so much on the side of the AI companies, the compensation falls short of what it should be. In the end, simple rules may have to prevail, distinguishing less amongst quality than say might be desirable. This is what is effectively done through a fixed scale of fees that are pre-determined, as is the case with pharmaceutical licensing or music royalties.

Code/Data excerpt: The public discussion also points to potential effects of GenAI on content industries, in particular online  news.1The worry is that AI-generated summaries of articles displace traffic to original sources, which  reduces revenues that are essential to producing content in the first place. Systematic evidence on how  AI summarisation, e.g. through technologies like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)2, affects  publishers is still limited. An early study suggests mixed effects (Duch-Brown et al., 2025): overall traffic  to news outlets remained stable after Google introduced “AI Overviews” in the US, compared to traffic in  the EU where the feature was not yet rolled out. When ChatGPT introduced links in answers, visits and  pageviews increased, while pageviews per visit decreased. These findings resonate with a well-studied  analogue: news aggregation platforms. When Google News introduced a localisation feature, traffic to  local news outlets increased (George and Hogendorn, 2020). After Google News shut down in Spain, visits  to news outlets decreased between 8% and 14% (Calzada and Gil, 2020; Athey et al., 2017). Similarly, after  Google News introduced an opt-in policy in Germany, visits to opted-in outlets increased by 8% (Calzada  and Gil, 2020). It is too early to come to strong conclusions, but the available evidence suggests that,  rather than diverting traffic away from outlets, GenAI has the potential to expand the news market, at  least on average. The related evidence, however, also suggests that the effects might be heterogeneous  across publisher size and type and more empirical work is needed to better inform the policy debate.

Code/Data excerpt: In theorising the journalism-audience relationship, Uth et al. (2023) described six categories, namely (1) discursive, (2) expectation-based, (3) network-oriented, (4) technological, (5) parasocial, and (6) strategic-organisational conceptualisations. In the network-oriented approach, the relationship between journalists and their audience is based on interactions and connections in a networked public, and this model considers audiences to be equal actors in journalistic production. The idea that journalists and the audience could connect with each other outside of content production, that there could be an emotional connection between them, or even that members of the audience could get to know each other, is not part of the theory. There are studies showing that belonging to a community plays an important role in news consumers’ content consumption and payment decisions. Chen and Thorson (2024) summarised the results of in-depth interviews and online surveys and identified six underlying motivations that drive people to pay for news: support for journalism, the quality of journalism, triggered by the paywall, community attachment, affordability, and content utility. Those who support local media often actually want to become part of the local community, to understand local problems, and to gain insight into local decision-making.

Code/Data excerpt: The real question is how enduring the role of communities can be. Currently, it is hard to predict this. It is conceivable that in the illiberal Hungarian regime, supporting independent media and participating in the relevant events is seen as an act of civic resistance of sorts, a form of protest against the political regime. In the extremely polarised Hungarian society, many may indeed find it important to belong to a community where they can talk about public affairs without conflict. A major question is therefore what would happen in the case that there is a major change in the underlying political situation. On the one hand, we do not know the direction in which the current Hungarian political and media system will develop, and under what regulatory and business environment media corporations will have to operate in the future. Furthermore, we also do not know how audiences will react to changes, how those might shape their trust in media, and whether the existing independent media will be able to retain their prestige and consumers will continue to be willing to support them. There is a real risk that many of those who have supported independent media up to this point might expect these media to be less critical towards a new government led by the current opposition, and that the media outlets abandon their watchdog function so that they do not constrain the new government’s freedom of action. It is even conceivable that in the event of changes in the political situation, the emergence of a more democratic and deliberative communication environment, the communities that have emerged around independent media organizations become less important and eventually disintegrate.

In February and March 2026, we conducted the first large-scale empirical audit of how AI models use and distribute Canadian journalism. We ran two studies. First, we tested four major AI models on 2,267 real Canadian news stories in both English and French (18,134 queries in total) to measure what models have absorbed from their training data and whether they attribute it. Second, we enabled web search and asked the same models
about 140 specific recent articles from seven Canadian outlets across 3,360 experimental conditions, to measure whether AI models produce viable substitutes for current journalism and whether they credit the source. When asked about Canadian news events drawn from their training data, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok provide no source attribution 82% of the time. When given web access and asked about specific recent arti-
cles, the same models covered enough of the original reporting to substitute for the source in 54 to 81% of cases. Models linked to Canadian news sites in 29 to 69% of responses, but named the originating outlet in the response text in only 1 to 16% of cases. When we named the outlet and asked the same models for citations, attribution rates reached 74–97%. The rules governing how these companies use journalism (who gets credited,who gets compensated, and what obligations attach to those who profit), are being set right now, by default,
through inaction.

Statutory licensing is structurally different from the bilateral bargaining model that underlies C-18. Rather than requiring AI companies to negotiate compensation with individual publishers, a statutory licence permits use by law while making payment mandatory, with rates set through a centralized mechanism rather than deal by deal. Policymakers in the EU, Indonesia, and LatinAmerica are developing versions of this model for AI training, and the World Intellectual Property Organization
has begun examining it as a global framework. The rationale is that it addresses two structural weaknesses of alternative approaches: bilateral deals tend to favor large publishers with the leverage to negotiate, while opt-out regimes are functionally unenforceable once content has been ingested into model weights. For Canadian journalism, where our data show that AI visibility is concentrated among a handful of large, nationally prominent outlets while regional and French-language newsrooms are largely invisible, this distributional question is central to any compensation framework. Whether a collective mechanism would produce more equitable outcomes than bilateral negotiation depends on design choices that have not yet been tested at scale.

AI models have absorbed Canadian news at scale and almost never say so. All four models showed knowledge of Canadian current events for stories inside their training windows. Wire ser-
vices and other public sources covering the same events may also contribute, but the pattern is consistent with having ingested Canadian news reporting.

Among responses where a model demonstrated that knowledge, 92% provided no source attribution of any kind: no named outlet, no recommendation, no reference.

• AI models substitute for the article and link to sources, but rarely name them. With web access, models covered enough distinctive reporting to re duce a consumer’s need to visit the source in 54% (ChatGPT) to 81% (Gemini) of cases. Models linked to Canadian news sites in 52% of responses. But they rarely named any Canadian source in the response text: 2% (Gemini) to 54% (ChatGPT) of responses. When directly prompted, naming rates reached 74% (Grok) to 97% (Claude).

• Paywalls do not protect content in a competitive news market. AI models covered paywalled content (64%) at rates comparable to free content (70%). For most stories, models find freely avail-
able versions elsewhere. In some cases, API logs showed models citing paywalled URLs directly with extensive verbatim reproduction, suggesting that paywalls may not block automated retrieval the way they block human readers. Either way, the result is the same: paywalled journalism is reproduced with-
out compensation.

• Naming sources is technically possible but rarely the default. When prompted, naming rates reached 74% (Grok) to 97% (Claude). Under default conditions, models linked to Canadian news sites 52% of the time but rarely named the outlet in the response text itself. Links let a consumer reach the source; naming would tell them whose journalism they are reading. The gap between the two is a design choice.
